verses.zh: 末后的日子，耶和华殿的山必坚立，超乎诸山，高举过于万岭；万民都要流归这山。
verses.en: And in future days[NOTE:1] the Lord’s Temple Mount will be the most important mountain of all;[NOTE:2] it will be more prominent than other hills.[NOTE:3] People will stream to it.
notes: Cf. Isa 2:2. See the note at Gen 49:1.
Heb “will be established as the head of the mountains.”
Heb “it will be lifted up above the hills.”
verses.commentary:
4:1,3-5 Notice the different speakers. This entire section is very similar to Isa. 2:2-4.

- These are words from Micah, as are Micah 4:9-13.

- In Micah 4:2 the nations speak,

- In Micah 4:6-8 YHWH speaks.

4:1

NASB
"In the last days"

NKJV, Peshitta
"In the latter days"

NRSV, REV, TEV, JPSOA
"In the days to come"

NJB
"But in the days to come"

NET
"In the future"

LXX
"As at the last days"

This phrase (BDB 31 [KB 35 I, #2] CONSTRUCT with BDB 398) is repeated often in the OT
(cf. Gen. 49:1; Num. 24:14; Deut. 4:30; 31:29; Isa. 2:2; Jer. 23:20; 30:24; 48:47; 49:39; Ezek. 38:16; Dan. 10:14; Hosea 3:5;
Micah 4:1).

BDB describes it in this way, "The final period of history so far as the speaker's perspective reaches.
It often equals the ideal or Messianic future."

The phrase has some variation:

- Dan. 2:28 ‒ BDB 1079 CONSTRUCT with BDB 1095 ("the end of days")

- Ezek. 38:8 ‒ BDB 31 CONSTRUCT with BDB 1040 ("the latter years")

- also in Ezekiel 38 the phrase is parallel to the famous prophetic phrase "that day" (cf. Ezek. 30:2-3;
38:10,14,18; 39:11; also Isa. 2:12; 10:3; 13:6,9; 34:2,8; 61:2; Jer. 30:7,8; Joel 1:15; 2:11,31; Amos 5:18;
Zeph. 1:14, 15, 16,18).

The rabbis of the interbiblical period developed a concept of two ages: the current evil age (begun
in Genesis 3) and an age of righteousness inaugurated by the Messiah (cf. Micah 3:12-13; 5:1-5a). However, from
further NT revelation (i.e. progressive revelation), we understand that the Messiah came not once, but twice (see Special
Topic below). The period from the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem until a Coming could be called the "last days."

The interpretive issue is when does this Coming occur?

- some temporal future coming (i.e. A.D. 70)

- before an earthly thousand year reign

- before the beginning of eternity?

Part of this question deals with how we view the future. Is it earth-like
(restored Garden of Eden, i.e. Genesis 1-2; Revelation 21-22; see Special Topic: Eden) or totally different
(cf. 1 Cor. 15:35-49)? Is the Bible literal (dispensational premillennial) or literary (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruninghooks)?

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT), III., IV., and VI.

Special Topic: That Day

Special Topic: Second Coming, IV.

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

▣ "the mountain of the house of the Lord" Jerusalem was built on seven
hills. The two major ones were Mt. Moriah, on which the temple stood, and Mt. Zion (i.e. site of the old Jebusite
fortress and David's palace; see Special Topic: Zion), which became literary imagery
for the whole city (cf. Micah 4:2).

The imagery of a mountain as the dwelling place of the gods is recurrent in Mesopotamian,
Canaanite, and even YHWH (cf. Ps. 48:2; 87; Isa. 14:13; Ezek. 28:14), and Greco-Roman literature.

There is an interesting article, "Divine Assembly," in Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, pp. 50-53 and also
"Mountain" (pp. 572-574). See Special Topic: Heavenly Council of Angelic Beings

- for Mesopotamia ‒ ziggurats (man-made mountains)

- for Canaan ‒ Mt. Zaphon

- for Hebrews

- Mt. Sinai

- Mt. Moriah/Zion

- "the mountain in the north" (i.e. Ps. 48:1-2; Isa. 14:13)

- for Greeks ‒ Mt. Olympus

Earlier Micah has just predicted the total destruction of Jerusalem and the temple (cf. Micah 3:12). Now he
asserts that YHWH's universal kingdom will come to fruition in Jerusalem. He will establish His reign on a renamed
Mt. Zion (i.e. "New Jerusalem," cf. Rev. 21; see full exegetical notes online). The ruined hill will become the most important mountain
on the earth (note the parallelism between lines 2, 3, and 4).

For the difference between OT prophecies about the future and NT prophecies, see full note at Micah 4:7 or
Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

▣ "It will be raised above the hills" This is figurative language representing the preeminence of the
temple in Jerusalem. Always Jewish people say, "Let us go up to Jerusalem." This concept is now widened into a
universal sense. Mt. Moriah is viewed as the highest, most significant elevation on the planet, that place that is closest to God!

▣ "the peoples will stream to it" Notice this wonderful universal element in Micah 4:1-3. This is a recurrent
theme in the OT (cf. Ps. 22:27; 66:4; 86:9; Isa. 2:2-4; 19:21,23; 27:13; 45:22-23; 50:6-8; 66:23; Jer. 3:17; 4:2; Zech. 2:11;
8:20-23; 14:16). See Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Notice how in the OT people come to God's mountain on the temple, but in the NT His people
are sent out (Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8). There is a new temple-Jesus (cf. John 2:19,21)-and by faith in Him
each believer becomes a temple (cf. 1 Cor. 6:19). Instead of coming to the temple in Jerusalem, the NT temples go to the nations! God's
universal, eternal, redemptive plan is now functioning!

Notice the startling contrast between Micah 3:12 (i.e. exile) and Micah 4:l (i.e. restoration and glorification). Also notice
the universal nature of the coming reign of the Messiah (cf. Micah 2:13; 5:2-5a). This universal aspect is so characteristic of Isaiah and Micah
(as well as Dan. 2:45; 7:9-10,13-14).

It is uncertain if the nations

- come once and go home

- come every year like a Jewish annual feast

It is to be noted that in a context of Neo-Babylonian exile (cf. Micah 4:10); the VERB "will stream"
(BDB 625, KB 676, Qal PERFECT with waw), is the same VERB Qal IMPERFECT)
used to describe the captive nations streaming away from Babylon in Jer. 51:44. Cyrus (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:3), YHWH's chosen vessel, allowed all the exiled
people to return home and funded the rebuilding of their national temples.

verses.zh: 必有许多国的民前往，说：来吧，我们登耶和华的山，奔雅各　神的殿。主必将他的道教训我们；我们也要行他的路。因为训诲必出于锡安；耶和华的言语必出于耶路撒冷。
verses.en: Many nations will come, saying,“Come on! Let’s go up to the Lord’s mountain,to the temple of Jacob’s God,so he can teach us his waysand we can live by his laws.”[NOTE:1] For instruction will proceed from Zion,the Lord’s message from Jerusalem.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and we can walk in his paths.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
verses.commentary:
4:2 "And many nations will come and say" Verse 2 records the supposed comment of the nations. All people
are welcome (e.g. Isa. 11:10; 49:22).

- if there is one God (i.e. monotheism, cf. 1 Kgs. 8:43,60)

- all humans are made in His image (cf. Gen. 1:26-27)

- He promises to redeem all mankind (cf. Gen. 3:15)

- then "one people" is the ultimate goal (cf. Gal. 3:23-29; Eph. 2:11-3:13). YHWH chose to reveal
Himself through national Israel, but ultimately through the ideal Israelite, His Servant (cf. Isa. 52:13-53:12),
His Son (cf. Psalm 2; 2 Samuel 7)

Verse 2 has several IMPERATIVES:

- "come" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "go" ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT

- "teach" ‒ BDB 434, KB 436, Hiphil IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning

- "walk" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal COHORTATIVE

The term "many" (cf. vv. 2,3) in the Bible often has the connotation of "all" (i.e. this is
the context of Micah 3:1-3).

- Isaiah 53

- "all," v. 6, lines 1 and 3

- "many," vv. 11d and 12e

- Romans 5

- v. 18, "all"

- v. 19, "many"

Special Topic: Monotheism

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Special Topic: Messiah

▣ "That he may teach us about His ways

And that we may walk in His paths" There are three aspects to biblical faith (cf. Ezra 7:10):

- knowing God (personal relationship)

- knowing God's will (Scripture, cf. Ps. 19:7-14; 119:1-176)

- living God's will (Scripture obedience, cf. Isa. 51:4-8)

This is like an OT Great Commission (compare Matt. 28:19-20, especially v. 20).

YHWH wants a people who reflect His character. His goal has always been to reach the world (cf. lines 6 & 7)!
Humans were created for fellowship with God (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:8)!

This is the opposite of Micah 3:6-7. Revelation is restored!

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

Special Topic: Terms for God's Revelation

verses.zh: 他必在多国的民中施行审判，为远方强盛的国断定是非。他们要将刀打成犁头，把枪打成镰刀。这国不举刀攻击那国；他们也不再学习战事。
verses.en: He will arbitrate[NOTE:1] between many peoplesand settle disputes between many[NOTE:2] distant nations.[NOTE:3] They will beat their swords into plowshares[NOTE:4] and their spears into pruning hooks.[NOTE:5] Nations will not use weapons[NOTE:6] against other nations,and they will no longer train for war.
notes: Or “judge.”
Or “mighty” (NASB); KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV “strong”; TEV “among the great powers.”
Heb “[for many nations] to a distance.”
Instead of referring to the large plow as a whole, the plowshare is simply the metal tip which actually breaks the earth and cuts the furrow.

This implement was used to prune the vines, i.e., to cut off extra leaves and young shoots (M. Klingbeil, NIDOTTE 1:1117-18). It was a short knife with a curved hook at the end sharpened on the inside like a sickle.
Heb “take up the sword.”
verses.commentary:
4:3 "And he will judge between many peoples" This is an extreme contrast between Judah's judicial actions
and YHWH's (cf. Micah 3:1, 9, 11). YHWH's judgments (i.e. Messiah's judgments [so Ibn Ezra], Isa. 11:3-5; Micah 5:4) will
result in social peace, not exploitation (cf. Isa. 2:2-4).

▣ "Then they will hammer their swords into plowshares

And their spears into pruning hooks" This is beautiful imagery to describe the peaceful
reign of the Messiah (i.e. note the synonymous parallelism of the next line of poetry, cf. Micah 5:5a;
Ps. 46:9, 76:3; Hosea 2:18; for the reverse imagery see Joel 3:10).

The exact nature of these agricultural implements is uncertain (BDB 88 III). They
were made of metal and were used, not like a wooden plow to turn over soil, but to scratch a furrow. It was
usually a metal tipped piece of sharpened wood.

Special Topic: Messianic Era

▣ "And never again will they train for war" The VERB "train" (BDB 540, KB 531,
Qal IMPERFECT) means to learn (e.g. Deut. 4:10; 17:19; Ps. 119:73). It can refer to warfare
(cf. 1 Chr. 5:18; Song of Songs 3:8). Not only is the coming restoration universal, it is also permanent (cf. Micah 4:5 line 3; 7 line 4).

verses.zh: 人人都要坐在自己葡萄树下和无花果树下，无人惊吓。这是万军之耶和华亲口说的。
verses.en: Each will sit under his own grapevineor under his own fig tree without any fear.[NOTE:1] The Lord of Heaven’s Armies has decreed it.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and there will be no one making [him] afraid.”
Heb “for the mouth of the Lord…has spoken.”
verses.commentary:
4:4 "And each of them will sit under his vine

And under his fig tree" Israel and Judah were agricultural societies. This idiom denoted a
peaceful and happy agricultural life. These phrases reflect the restoration of all the covenant descendants of Abraham back to the
Promised Land, where each had their family land given by lot in Josshua 12-19 restored (cf. 1 Kgs. 4:25; Isa. 36:16; Zech. 3:10).
This was meant to be a regular event (i.e. Year of Jubilee), but God's people never implemented it.

Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.

▣ "With no one to make them afraid" In the OT if God's people live in light of His promises and
covenant (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28), He will defend them (cf. Lev. 26:3-6).

This text in Micah reflects the Messiah's presence and rule (which reflects an eschatological setting).

▣ "For the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken" This speaks of the
power and trustworthiness of YHWH's Word (cf. Isa. 40:5,8; 45:23; 55:11). His promises and trustworthiness are the
basis of mankind's hope and faith (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:56).

The title, "Lord of hosts," in a context relates to Israel and Judah. YHWH is the
commander and leader of the army of angels (i.e. Josh. 5:13-15). In some contexts (i.e. Mesopotamian astral worship) "hosts" refers
to the pagan theory of gods/angels behind the lights in the sky (i.e. planets, stars, constellations, comets, etc.) that control human lives.

Special Topic: Anthropomorphic Language to Describe God

Special Topic: Angels in the Bible

Special Topic: Lord of Hosts

verses.zh: 万民各奉己神的名而行；我们却永永远远奉耶和华―我们　神的名而行。
verses.en: Though all the nations follow their respective gods,[NOTE:1] we will follow[NOTE:2] the Lord our God forever.
notes: Heb “walk each in the name of his god.” The term “name” here has the idea of “authority.” To “walk in the name” of a god is to recognize the god’s authority as binding over one’s life.
Heb “walk in the name of.”
verses.commentary:
4:5 This verse seems to be out of context. This is a strange verse in a context which speaks of the universal
and permanent reign of the one true God, YHWH of Israel. Some see it as:

- This glorious future is not here yet because currently every nation has its own god (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:29).

- Not all people of all the nations would recognize YHWH even in a future ideal time (e.g. Rev. 22:15).

- This is an affirmation of those from the nations who have come to Jerusalem (cf. Micah 4:1e, 2a, 3a,b) and now affirm YHWH their
sovereign and God forever.

The tension in this chapter between "believing nations" and "unbelieving nations" is seen in the
contrast between Micah 4:1-4 and Micah 4:5!

Special Topic: "The Name" of YHWH (OT)

Special Topic: Seek the Lord

Special Topic: Call On His Name

verses.zh: 耶和华说：到那日，我必聚集瘸腿的，招聚被赶出的和我所惩治的。
verses.en: “In that day,” says the Lord, “I will gather the lameand assemble the outcasts whom I injured.[NOTE:1]
notes: The exiles of the nation are compared to lame and injured sheep.
verses.commentary:
4:6-8 This continues the theme of earlier chapters in Micah, YHWH as shepherd (cf. Micah 2:12-13, Ps. 23; Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34),
who cares for those who society has rejected (cf. Isa. 35:5-6; 61:1-2; Jer. 31:8; Zeph. 3:19). No one is left out or left behind!

- the lame (BDB 854 II, cf. Zeph. 3:19)

- the outcast (BDB 623, KB 673, Niphal PARTICIPLE)

- those far away (MT, v. 7, BDB 229, KB 245, Niphal PARTICIPLE)

Special Topic: That Day

4:6 "In that day" See note at Micah 4:1.

▣ "lame" This word means "limping flock" or "wounded sheep" (BDB 854 II). This is prophetic
imagery for divine help (cf. Zeph. 3:19). It was used of Jacob in his encounter with the angel in Gen. 32:24-32.

There is obviously a parallel between v. and v. 7.

▣ "assemble" As lame and outcast are parallel, so too, the VERBS:

- "assemble" ‒ BDB 62, KB 74, Qal COHORTATIVE

- "gather" ‒ BDB 867, KB 1062, Piel COHORTATIVE

▣ "outcasts" This refers literally to sheep who have left the flock (i.e. banished ones, BDB 621,
KB 673, Niphal PARTICIPLE, cf. Zeph. 3:19).

The NASB translates two different Hebrew PARTICIPLES as "outcasts"

- BDB 623, KB 673, Niphal PARTICIPLE, v. 6, cf. Zeph. 3:19

- BDB 229, KB 245, Niphal PARTICIPLE, v. 7

but #2 literally means "to be far off" (NET, Peshitta). See full note at v. 7.

▣ "Even those whom I have afflicted" YHWH Himself brought judgment on His people by the means of
pagan nations (here the exiled "lame" and "outcast"; see Special Topic: The Second Coming, IV.)
in order to bring them back to the place of personal faith. God disciplines those who are part of His family (cf. Heb. 12:5ff).

The Assyrians killed the weak and lame, the old and very young. Not so with YHWH, the Shepherd of Israel (cf. Ps. 23; Jesus in John 10).

verses.zh: 我必使瘸腿的为余剩之民，使赶到远方的为强盛之民。耶和华要在锡安山作王治理他们，从今直到永远。
verses.en: I will transform the lame into the nucleus of a new nation[NOTE:1] and those far off[NOTE:2] into a mighty nation.The Lord will reign over them on Mount Zion,from that day forward and forevermore.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “make the lame into a remnant.”

The precise meaning of this difficult form is uncertain. The present translation assumes the form is a Niphal participle of an otherwise unattested denominative verb הָלָא (halaʾ, “to be far off”; see BDB 229 s.v.), but attractive emendations include הַנַּחֲלָה (hannakhalah, “the sick one[s]”) from חָלָה (khalah) and הַנִּלְאָה (hannilʾah, “the weary one[s]”) from לָאָה (laʾah).
Heb “from now until forever.”
verses.commentary:
4:7 "a remnant. . .a strong nation" YHWH always starts with a small group (e.g. Adam and Eve, Noah,
Abraham, Moses, etc.), but this small group of believers is meant to become more than the stars of heaven, the
sands of the sea, and the dust of the earth (see full list as Gen. 15:5). They (believers in YHWH) are
meant to fill the earth.

YHWH Himself or His Messiah will gather and accomplish this universal task (Ezek. 36:22-38). God's
plan has always included all human beings (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6).

- in Genesis the Garden of Eden is the special place

- in Exodus ‒ Joshua the Promised Land is the special place

- in the prophets Jerusalem is the special place

- in the NT it is New Jerusalem coming down out of heaven (i.e. Rev. 21)

For the theological implications to "remnant" see Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses)

Special Topic: Immanuel's Person and Reign

Special Topic: YHWH's Etermal Redemptive Plan

▣

NASB, NKJV, REB
"the outcasts"

NRSV
"those who were cast off"

TEV
"those who are left"

NJB
"the far-flung"

JPSOA
"the expelled"

NIV, LXX, Peshitta
"those driven away"

NAB
"those driven off"

The Hebrew text is uncertain. Several emendations have been suggested:

- MT's הלא, BDB 229, KB 245, "outcasts," "those who are far off"

- חלה, BDB 317, "sick" (JPSOA footnote suggests Ezek. 34:4 as an example)

- לאה, BDB 521, "weary"

▣ "the Lord will reign over them in Mount Zion" There is a literary parallel
between "reigning" and "shepherding" in the ANE (e.g. shepherd, Micah 5:4,6 and reign, Micah 4:7; 5:12).

Special Topic: Why Are OT Covenant Promises So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

Special Topic: Zion

▣ "From now on and forever" This parallels Micah 4:5d. YHWH's promises are sure. God's plans are permanent. However,

- There is a progressive revelation; the OT has been fulfilled by the NT (i.e. Matt. 5:17-19).

- Unconditional and conditional covenants, see Special Topic: Covenant

God reveals Himself in fuller ways and categories, but the goal is always life with Him!

For the concept of "forever," see Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios)

verses.zh: 你这羊群的高台、锡安城（原文是女子）的山哪，从前的权柄―就是耶路撒冷民（原文是女子）的国权―必归与你。
verses.en: As for you, watchtower for the flock,[NOTE:1] fortress of Daughter Zion[NOTE:2]—your former dominion will be restored,[NOTE:3] the sovereignty that belongs to Daughter Jerusalem.”
notes: Heb “Migdal Eder.” Some English versions transliterate this phrase, apparently because they view it as a place name (cf. NAB).

The city of David, located within Jerusalem, is addressed as Daughter Zion. As the home of the Davidic king, who was Israel’s shepherd (Ps 78:70-72), the royal citadel could be viewed metaphorically as the watchtower of the flock.
Heb “to you it will come, the former dominion will arrive.”
verses.commentary:
4:8 "tower of the flock" This is possibly

- a special place name near Bethlehem itself, where sacrificial sheep for daily sacrifice were raised
(i.e. Jerome and possibly Gen. 35:21 or Migdal-eder, JPSOA). This will become the focus of prophecy in
Micah 5:2 (cf. Luke 2:8-20), which relates to the Messiah's (who is the sinless Lamb of God, cf. John 1:29) birthplace where
the daily lambs for sacrifice (i.e. the Continual) are kept year round by Levitical shepherds.

- it refers to the king/shepherd watching over his people from the capital (here it is God or His Messiah). See
Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

It is possible, using poetic synonymous parallelism, to understand several phrases:

- "in Mount Zion," Micah 4:7 line 3

- "tower of the flock," Micah 4:8 line 1

- "hill of the daughter of Zion," Micah 4:8, line 2 (cf. Micah 4:10,13)

- "the daughter of Jerusalem," Micah 4:8 line 5

as all referring to the capital of Judah (i.e. Jerusalem, cf. Isa. 24:23).

▣ "Hill of the daughter of Zion" This is possibly another place name, Ophel (BDB 779 I).
Ophel was the district of Jerusalem where David's palace was located. It may be an allusion to a restored
Davidic dynasty (cf. 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17).

For more information of "daughter of . . ." see notes at Amos 5:2 and Jer. 46:11.

▣ "Even the former dominion will come" This section may reflect Isa. 1:24-26. After Judah is judged, she
will be restored to her previous greatness. This, of course, is imagery for restoration because, in reality, her
future is far more extensive (i.e. universal, cf. Micah 5:4; Ps. 2:8; 22:27-28; 59:13; 72:8) than her past
(i.e. kingdom of David and Solomon).

verses.zh: 现在你为何大声哭号呢？疼痛抓住你彷佛产难的妇人，是因你中间没有君王吗？你的谋士灭亡了吗？
verses.en: Jerusalem, why are you[NOTE:1] now shouting so loudly?[NOTE:2] Has your king disappeared?[NOTE:3] Has your wise leader[NOTE:4] been destroyed?Is this why[NOTE:5] pain grips[NOTE:6] you as if you were a woman in labor?
notes: The Hebrew form is feminine singular, indicating that Jerusalem, personified as a young woman, is now addressed (see v. 10). In v. 8 the tower/fortress was addressed with masculine forms, so there is clearly a shift in addressee here. “Jerusalem” has been supplied in the translation at the beginning of v. 9 to make this shift apparent.
Heb “Now why are you shouting [with] a shout.”
Heb “Is there no king over you?”

Traditionally, “counselor” (cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV84, NRSV); NIV11 “ruler.” This refers to the king mentioned in the previous line; the title points to the king’s roles as chief strategist and policy maker, both of which required extraordinary wisdom.
Heb “that.” The Hebrew particle כִּי (ki) is used here in a resultative sense; for this use see R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 73, §450.
Heb “grabs hold of, seizes.”
verses.commentary:
4:9-13 The historical setting is again ambiguous, but because of Micah 4:10, it seems to reflect the destruction of Jerusalem in
586 B.C. by Neo-Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II.

Special Topic: Kings of Neo-Babylon

4:9 "why do you cry out so loudly" This refers to the time of exile (see Jer. 8:19). The "you" is FEMININE
SINGULAR and refers to Jerusalem or Judah.

▣ "Is there no king among you" This seems to be a sarcastic comment on chapter 3. The king was
God's representative, and yet, if the king is evil, to whom can the people turn?

▣ "has your counselor perished" King and counselor are parallel and refer to the head of the
royal line. In Isa. 9:6 it is one of several titles of the coming Messianic king (see Isa. 3:1-3). Here it relates back to the
false religious leaders of Micah 3:5-7.

Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

▣ "like a woman in childbirth" Birthing (cf. Micah 4:10 lines 1-3) is OT imagery for judgment
and pain (cf. Isa. 42:14; Jer. 4:31; 6:24). In Mark 13:8 and Rom. 8:22 it is used of the birth pangs of the New Age
(i.e. for ever and ever).

Special Topic: Birth Pains

verses.zh: 锡安的民（原文是女子）哪，你要疼痛劬劳，彷佛产难的妇人；因为你必从城里出来，住在田野，到巴比伦去。在那里要蒙解救；在那里耶和华必救赎你脱离仇敌的手。
verses.en: Twist and strain,[NOTE:1] Daughter Zion, as if you were in labor!For you will leave the cityand live in the open field.You will go to Babylon,but there you will be rescued.There the Lord will deliver[NOTE:2] youfrom the power[NOTE:3] of your enemies.
notes: Or perhaps “scream”; NRSV, TEV, NLT “groan.”
Or “redeem” (KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
Heb “hand.” The Hebrew idiom is a metonymy for power or control.
verses.commentary:
4:10

NASB, Peshitta
"Writhe and labor to bring forth"

NKJV
"be in pain and labor to bring forth"

NRSV
"writhe and groan"

TEV
"twist and groan"

NJB
"writhe in pain and cry aloud"

LXX
"suffer pain, be courageous"

JPSOA
"writhe and scream"

Both of these VERBS ("writhe" BDB 296, KB 297, and "labor," lit. "burst forth,"
BDB 161, KB 189) are Qal IMPERATIVES.

▣ "For now you will go out of the city, Dwell in the field" This is specifically referring to a forced exile
after the capture of Jerusalem. These people will be forced to live out of doors while they are being marched to new
homes and fields far away in Babylon.

▣ "And go to Babylon" This is a specific allusion to the powerful Mesopotamian nation that
conquered Assyria and the Fertile Crescent. Assyria took captive the Northern Ten Tribes (Israel) in 722 B.C.
(cf. chapters 1-2). Neo-Babylon took captive the southern tribes (Judah) in 586 B B.C. (cf. Micah 3:12).

Many scholars are surprised at such a specific reference to Neo-Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs. 20:18). This same non-chronological
aspect can be seen in Isaiah 13-14. However, it must also be mentioned that Babylon can be a general way of referring to
Mesopotamia, for there was a Babylonian Empire before Assyria (i.e. Old Babylon) and even long before that (cf. Gen. 10:10).

It could also be imagery, following Gen. 11:4-9, referring to anti-God world powers (like Daniel 2; 7; 8). This would follow
John the Apostle's use in the book of the Revelation (cf. Rev. 14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2,10,21).

▣ "There you will be rescued;

There the Lord will redeem you

From the hand of your enemies" Here is another glimpse of hope (lines 7-9) amidst the blackness of judgment
(lines 1-6). There is another radical subject break after Micah 4:10. The new subject is introduced in Micah 4:11-12. The text moves from
deliverance to another future attack beyond their return from Babylon (i.e. Dan. 9:24-27; Ezekiel 38-39). I think it refers to the destruction of Jerusalem
and the temple by Rome in A.D. 70. See my exegetical notes free online involving Jesus' Olivet Discourse, Paul's "Man of
Lawlessness," and John's book of Revelation.

Special Topic: Ransom/Redeem

▣ "From the hand of your enemies" "Hand" was an idiom for power.

Special Topic: Hand

notes: Heb “let her be desecrated.” The referent (Jerusalem) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and let our eye look upon Zion.” This is a Hebrew idiom for a typically smug or condescending look by someone in a superior position.
verses.commentary:
4:11 "now many nations have been assembled against you" This seems to refer to the mercenary troops found both in the Assyrian
(e.g. Sennacherib, 701 B.C.) and Neo-Babylonian armies (e.g. Nebuchadnezzar, 586 B.C.). One example of these
mercenaries is Edom, specifically stated in Obadiah.

However, those who are looking for a certain pre-millennial position often find credence in
their position from passages like this in the Prophets.

verses.zh: 他们却不知道耶和华的意念，也不明白他的筹划。他聚集他们，好像把禾捆聚到禾场一样。
verses.en: But they do not know what the Lord is planning;they do not understand his strategy.He has gathered them like stalks of grain to be threshed[NOTE:1] at the threshing floor.
notes: The words “to be threshed” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation to make it clear that the Lord is planning to enable “Daughter Zion” to “thresh” her enemies.
verses.commentary:
4:12 When those who do not know YHWH or His Word view history, they see Him judging His own people. They
miss the goal of a special covenant people as a means for all people to know God. Abraham's descendants did not keep
the covenant, did not reveal God, so God chose to reveal Himself (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

In this chapter the tension between believing nations vs. attacking, unbelieving
nations is accentuated. The poetry is brief and ambiguous. It is difficult (impossible) to systematize it. These are
flashes of truth, of future events, or literary imagery. Three great truths are taught:

- YHWH's will of a restored believing humanity will be a reality.

- Some will not believe and will attack God by attacking His people.

- One group will be with God forever; one group will be destroyed (possibly origin of v. 5)!

▣ "He has gathered them" This seems to imply that God has gathered Israel's and Judah's enemies
to allow her to destroy them (cf. Micah 4:13; Isaiah 13-14; Ezekiel 38-39; Joel 4; Zechariah 14).

verses.zh: 锡安的民（原文是女子）哪，起来踹谷吧！我必使你的角成为铁，使你的蹄成为铜。你必打碎多国的民，将他们的财献与耶和华，将他们的货献与普天下的主。
verses.en: “Get up and thresh, Daughter Zion!For I will give you iron horns;[NOTE:1] I will give you bronze hooves,and you will crush many nations.”[NOTE:2] You will devote to the Lord the spoils you take from themand dedicate their wealth to the sovereign Ruler[NOTE:3] of the whole earth.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “I will make your horn iron.”
Jerusalem (Daughter Zion at the beginning of the verse; cf. 4:8) is here compared to a powerful ox which crushes the grain on the threshing floor with its hooves.
Or “the Lord” (so many English versions); Heb “the master.”

In vv. 11-13 the prophet jumps from the present crisis (which will result in exile, v. 10) to a time beyond the restoration of the exiles when God will protect his city from invaders. The Lord’s victory over the Assyrian armies in 701 b.c. foreshadowed this.tn Heb “and their wealth to the master of all the earth.” The verb “devote” does double duty in the parallelism and is supplied in the second line for clarification.
verses.commentary:
4:13 Verses 12-13 must be taken together to understand YHWH's comment. He calls His restored covenant
people to devastate those pagan nations which He used to punish His own people for their sins (cf. Micah 4:12;
Isa. 41:15-16; Jer. 51:20-23; Habakkuk).

The first two VERBS ("arise" BDB 877, KB 1086 and "thresh" BDB 190, KB 218)
are both Qal IMPERATIVES.

But in Micah 4:13 YHWH is speaking to His restored covenant people (i.e. New Covenant, cf. Jer. 31:31-34).
One day His people will be victorious. God wanted to use Abraham's descendants. He wanted the world to know Him
and come to Him, but Abraham's seed did not and the world could not!

▣ "That you may devote. . .their unjust gain

And their wealth to the Lord" This is imagery taken from
"holy war" (i.e. Jericho). YHWH's people avenging themselves on the very nations that devastated her by YHWH's
help was seen as the nations' wealth being given to YHWH because it is "holy" (i.e. herem).

Special Topic: Curse

▣ "to the Lord of all the earth" Again, notice this universal emphasis. In
context this chapter relates to YHWH's first covenant people, but in light of Jesus, it refers to the New Covenant people!

The doctrines of YHWH as Creator and the assertion of monotheism demands a worldwide emphasis!

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must
walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired,
but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BACKGROUND STUDY

- Micah 4:1-3 is very similar to Isa. 2:2-3. It is obvious that literary borrowing has occurred from one or
the other or they both borrowed from a third source.

- This chapter (vv. 1-8) wonderfully predicts the fulfillment of Gen. 3:15. The redemption and fellowship
of all peoples with their Creator is clearly asserted (cf. Isa. 2:23; and

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan).

But before this great day, tragedy and judgment on Israel and Judah will occur by divine decree (cf. vv. 9-12; also note Dan. 9:24-27).
However, YHWH will empower His people to overcome their enemies (i.e. in this context, Assyria and Neo-Babylon, cf. v. 13).

- The book of Micah seems to reflect two historical dates, as well as an eschatological position.
Throughout the book, either

- the Syro-Ephramatic War (i.e. the military alliance of Syria and Israel) of 735 B.C.
is the background

- the invasion of Judah by Sennacherib the Assyrian King in 701 B.C. However, at the
beginning of chapter 4, we realize that these two historical crises foreshadowed

- the later Neo-Babylonian invasions of Judah (Micah 4:10) occurred in 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.

- the ultimate crisis of history, the Kingdom of God vs. the kingdom of evil. See my exegetical notes on Matt. 24 and the
book of Revelation (2024).

- Several questions are left unanswered!

- Does any OT prophet see the two comings of the Messiah?

- Does this refer to

(1) a Jewish oriented millennium

(2) a church oriented eternity?

- Are the nations becoming believers and followers of YHWH (Micah 4:1-4) and/or His Messiah
or are they enemies to the bitter end (Micah 4:11-13)?

- Books that have been very helpful to me in trying to interpret prophecy in its historical setting are

- R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the OT

- Douglas Stuart and Gordon Fee, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth, pp. 181-204

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic
